text: Now that you can declare variables and know the types they hold, it's time to make decisions with them. This lesson covers comparison and logical operators, branching with if and switch, and the two main kinds of loops.

JavaScript has two equality operators, and they behave very differently. Double equals converts both sides to a common type before comparing, so the string one and the number one end up equal. Triple equals skips that conversion entirely - it checks type and value together, so the string one and the number one are not equal. ServiceNow scripting style strongly favors triple equals almost everywhere, specifically to avoid that kind of silent, surprising conversion.

Three operators combine or invert conditions. The double ampersand, meaning AND, is only true if both sides are true. The double pipe, meaning OR, is true if at least one side is true. And the exclamation mark flips a value to its opposite. Both AND and OR also short-circuit - they stop evaluating the moment the overall result is already decided, which matters if the right-hand side is a function call you don't want to run unnecessarily.

An if statement runs its block when its condition is true. Each else if is only checked when every condition above it was false, and else is the catch-all when nothing matched. When you're comparing one value against many specific possibilities, a switch statement is often clearer than a long chain of else-ifs - but remember to add a break after each case, or execution falls through into the next one.

A for loop is the standard choice when you know how many times you need to repeat something - like walking through an array of ticket numbers from the first index to the last. A while loop instead repeats for as long as a condition stays true, which fits better when you don't know the exact number of repetitions ahead of time, like retrying an operation until it succeeds or you hit a limit.

Strict equality, short-circuiting logic, and two loop styles - the building blocks every script you write from here forward will lean on. Next up: functions, where you'll package this logic so you can reuse it instead of repeating it.
